claim: Continual learning remains an unsolved problem in artificial neural networks.
source: Continual learning remains an unsolved problem in artificial neural networks.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of artificial neural networks without specific supporting data in the manuscript itself.

claim: The brain has evolved mechanisms to prevent catastrophic forgetting of old knowledge during new training.
source: The brain has evolved mechanisms to prevent catastrophic forgetting of old knowledge during new training.
evidence: This is a general statement about biological systems based on established scientific understanding.

claim: In the thalamocortical model, training a new memory interfered with previously learned old memories leading to degradation and forgetting of the old memory traces.
source: In the thalamocortical model, training a new memory interfered with previously learned old memories leading to degradation and forgetting of the old memory traces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental results from the computational model presented in the manuscript, specifically shown in Figure 4.

claim: Simulating sleep after new learning reversed the damage and enhanced old and new memories.
source: Simulating sleep after new learning reversed the damage and enhanced old and new memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: When a new memory competed for previously allocated neuronal/synaptic resources, sleep replay changed the synaptic footprint of the old memory to allow overlapping neuronal populations to store multiple memories.
source: We found that when a new memory competed for previously allocated neuronal/synaptic resources, sleep replay changed the synaptic footprint of the old memory to allow overlapping neuronal populations to store multiple memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of synaptic weight changes during sleep shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Memory storage is dynamic.
source: Our study predicts that memory storage is dynamic, and sleep enables continual learning by combining consolidation of new memory traces with reconsolidation of old memory traces to minimize interference.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results and analysis presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Sleep enables continual learning by combining consolidation of new memory traces with reconsolidation of old memory traces to minimize interference.
source: Our study predicts that memory storage is dynamic, and sleep enables continual learning by combining consolidation of new memory traces with reconsolidation of old memory traces to minimize interference.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the computational modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Training a new task results in interference and catastrophic forgetting of old memories in modern artificial neural networks.
source: Training a new task results in interference and catastrophic forgetting of old memories (Ratcliff, 1990; McClelland et al., 1995; French, 1999; Hasselmo, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on catastrophic forgetting in artificial neural networks.

claim: Several attempts have been made to overcome catastrophic forgetting including explicit retraining of all previously learned memories (interleaved training).
source: Several attempts have been made to overcome this problem including (a) explicit retraining of all previously learned memories – interleaved training (Hasselmo, 2017), (b) using generative models to reactivate previous inputs (Kemker and Kanan, 2017), or (c) artificially 'freezing' subsets of synapses important for the old memories (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on methods to address catastrophic forgetting.

claim: Sleep has been suggested to play an important role in learning and memory.
source: Sleep has been suggested to play an important role in learning and memory (Paller and Voss, 2004; Walker and Stickgold, 2004; Oudiette et al., 2013; Rasch and Born, 2013; Stickgold, 2013; Weigenand et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on sleep and memory.

claim: The role of stage 2 (N2) and stage 3 (N3) of Non-Rapid Eye Movement (NREM) sleep has been shown to help with the consolidation of newly encoded memories.
source: Specifically, the role of stage 2 (N2) and stage 3 (N3) of Non-Rapid Eye Movement (NREM) sleep has been shown to help with the consolidation of newly encoded memories (Paller and Voss, 2004; Walker and Stickgold, 2004; Rasch and Born, 2013; Stickgold, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on NREM sleep and memory consolidation.

claim: Sleep may enable memory consolidation through repeated reactivation or replay of specific memory traces during characteristic sleep rhythms such as spindles and slow oscillations.
source: Sleep may enable memory consolidation through repeated reactivation or replay of specific memory traces during characteristic sleep rhythms such as spindles and slow oscillations (Paller and Voss, 2004; Clemens et al., 2005; Marshall et al., 2006; Oudiette et al., 2013; Rasch and Born, 2013; Weigenand et al., 2016; Ladenbauer et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on memory replay during sleep.

claim: Increasing neocortical oscillations during NREM sleep resulted in improved consolidation of declarative memories.
source: Previous work using electrical (Marshall et al., 2004; Marshall et al., 2006; Ladenbauer et al., 2017) or auditory (Ngo et al., 2013) stimulation showed that increasing neocortical oscillations during NREM sleep resulted in improved consolidation of declarative memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work on sleep stimulation and memory.

claim: Spatial memory consolidation has been shown to improve following cued reactivation of memory traces during NREM sleep.
source: Similarly, spatial memory consolidation has been shown to improve following cued reactivation of memory traces during NREM sleep (Paller and Voss, 2004; Oudiette et al., 2013; Oudiette and Paller, 2013; Papalambros et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on cued memory reactivation during sleep.

claim: Sleep dynamics can lead to replay and strengthening of recently learned memory traces.
source: Our recent computational studies found that sleep dynamics can lead to replay and strengthening of recently learned memory traces (Wei et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2018; Wei et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' prior computational modeling work.

claim: Implementation of a sleep-like phase in artificial networks trained using backpropagation can dramatically reduce catastrophic forgetting, as well as improve generalization performance and transfer of knowledge.
source: We recently found that implementation of a sleep-like phase in artificial networks trained using backpropagation can dramatically reduce catastrophic forgetting, as well as improve generalization performance and transfer of knowledge (Krishnan et al., 2019; Tadros et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' prior work on sleep-like phases in artificial networks.

claim: The network model represents a minimal thalamocortical architecture implementing one cortical layer (consisting of excitatory pyramidal (PY) and inhibitory (IN) neurons) and one thalamic layer (consisting of excitatory thalamic relay (TC) and inhibitory reticular thalamic (RE) neurons).
source: The network model, used in our study, represents a minimal thalamocortical architecture implementing one cortical layer (consisting of excitatory pyramidal (PY) and inhibitory (IN) neurons) and one thalamic layer (consisting of excitatory thalamic relay (TC) and inhibitory reticular thalamic (RE) neurons) – with all neurons simulated by Hodgkin-Huxley models (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim describes the model architecture used in the study, which is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The model exhibits two primary dynamical states of the thalamocortical system – awake, characterized by random asynchronous firing of all cortical neurons, and slow-wave sleep (SWS), characterized by slow (<1 Hz) oscillations between Up (active) and Down (silent) states.
source: This model exhibits two primary dynamical states of the thalamocortical system – awake, characterized by random asynchronous firing of all cortical neurons, and slow-wave sleep (SWS), characterized by slow (<1 Hz) oscillations between Up (active) and Down (silent) states (Blake and Gerard, 1937; Steriade et al., 1993; Steriade et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim describes the model's behavior and is supported by citations to prior work on brain states and by the model results shown in Figure 1B/C.

claim: Transitions between sleep and awake were simulated by changing network parameters to model effect of neuromodulators.
source: Transitions between sleep and awake (Figure 1B/C) were simulated by changing network parameters to model effect of neuromodulators (Krishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim describes a methodological aspect of the model, supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1B/C.

claim: Only cortical PY-PY connections were plastic and regulated by spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP).
source: Only cortical PY-PY connections were plastic and regulated by spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP).
evidence: This claim describes a key feature of the model implementation.

claim: During initial training, STDP was biased for potentiation to simulate elevated levels of acetylcholine.
source: During initial training, STDP was biased for potentiation to simulate elevated levels of acetylcholine (Blokland, 1995; Shinoe et al., 2005; Sugisaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim describes a modeling choice supported by citations to prior work on acetylcholine effects.

claim: Training of spatially separated memory sequences S1 and S2 resulted in an increase of synaptic weights between participating neurons and an increase in performance on sequence completion.
source: Training S1 resulted in an increase of synaptic weights between participating neurons (Figure 2D, left) and an increase in performance on sequence completion (Figure 2B/C, top).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Training of S2 did not interfere with the weight changes encoding S1 because both sequences involved spatially distinct populations of neurons.
source: Importantly, training of S2 did not interfere with the weight changes encoding S1 because both sequences involved spatially distinct populations of neurons (compare Figure 2D, left and middle).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: After sleep, synaptic weights for both memory sequences revealed strong increases in the direction of their respective activation patterns and further decreases in the opposing directions.
source: After sleep, synaptic weights for both memory sequences revealed strong increases in the direction of their respective activation patterns and further decreases in the opposing directions (Figure 2D, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Synaptic strengthening increased the performance on sequence completion after sleep.
source: Synaptic strengthening increased the performance on sequence completion after sleep (Figure 2B, right; 2C, red bar).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: SWS following linear track training would lead to further receptive field backwards expansion in the cortical neurons.
source: This predicts that SWS following linear track training would lead to further receptive field backwards expansion in the cortical neurons.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The directionality index increased from naive to trained cortical networks and further increased after sleep.
source: This analysis showed an increase in the directionality index from naive to trained cortical networks and further increase after sleep (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The backwards expansion of the place fields was reset between sessions in CA1, but not in CA3.
source: Note, that the backwards expansion of the place fields was reset between sessions in CA1 (Mehta et al., 1997), but not in CA3 (Roth et al., 2012), where the backward shift gradually diminished across days, possibly as memories became hippocampus independent (see Discussion).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work on place fields in hippocampus.

claim: Memory patterns trained in awake are spontaneously replayed during sleep.
source: The hypothesis is that memory patterns trained in awake are spontaneously replayed during sleep.
evidence: This is the hypothesis being tested, which is then supported by the analysis in Figure 3.

claim: There is a strong positive correlation between the total change of synaptic strength across entire sleep and the number of Up states when that synapse was replayed.
source: Figure 3A shows, for each synapse in the direction of S1, the total change of its synaptic strength across entire sleep (Y-axis) vs number of Up states when that synapse was replayed (X-axis). As expected, it shows a strong positive correlation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There were multiple direct and indirect synaptic pathways connecting the first (A) and last (E) groups of neurons that were replayed reliably during sleep.
source: We concluded that there were multiple direct and indirect synaptic pathways connecting the first (A) and last (E) groups of neurons that were replayed reliably during sleep.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: These synapses increased their strength which explains reliable memory recall during testing after sleep.
source: These synapses increased their strength which explains reliable memory recall during testing after sleep.
evidence: This is an inference based on the replay analysis and performance results.

claim: Training S1 increased performance of S1 completion and led to decrease in performance for S1* below its baseline level in the 'naive' network.
source: In the model, training S1 increased performance of S1 completion (Figure 4C, top/left). It also led to decrease in performance for S1* below its baseline level in the 'naive' network (Figure 4C, bottom/left).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Subsequent training of S1* resulted in both a significant increase in S1* performance and a significant reduction of S1 performance.
source: Subsequent training of S1* resulted in both a significant increase in S1* performance and a significant reduction of S1 performance (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Increasing the duration of S1* training correlated with a reduction of S1 performance up to the point when S1 performance was reduced to its baseline level.
source: Increasing the duration of S1* training correlated with a reduction of S1 performance up to the point when S1 performance was reduced to its baseline level (Figures 4D and 400 sec training duration of S1*).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Sequential training of two memories competing for the same population of neurons results in memory interference and catastrophic forgetting of the earlier memory sequence.
source: This suggests that sequential training of two memories competing for the same population of neurons results in memory interference and catastrophic forgetting of the earlier memory sequence.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results shown in Figure 4.

claim: In experiments with a rat running forward and backward on a linear track, spatial sequences of opposite direction are rapidly orthogonalized in the hippocampus.
source: While we are not aware of such experiments, studies done with a rat running forward and backward on a liner track (Navratilova et al., 2012), which would be equivalent to interleaved training S1→ S1*→ S1→ S1*…., revealed that, in the hippocampus, spatial sequences of opposite direction are rapidly orthogonalized, largely on the basis of differential head direction system input, to accommodate both trainings.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: At each location, some neurons had their receptive field expanded in one direction and others in the opposite direction.
source: Thus, at each location, some neurons had their receptive field expanded in one direction and others in the opposite direction (Navratilova et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Interleaved training of S1 and S1* resulted in performance increase for both sequences.
source: To compare our model with these data, we tested interleaved training of S1 and S1* (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and found performance increase for both sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Different neurons became specific for S1 vs S1* as reflected in the overall increase of the directionality index during interleaved training.
source: Importantly, in agreement with in vivo data, different neurons became specific for S1 vs S1* as reflected in the overall increase of the directionality index (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Sleep improves sequence completion performance for all three memories, including competing memory traces – S1 and S1*.
source: We found that sleep improves sequence completion performance for all three memories, including competing memory traces – S1 and S1*. Figure 5B shows raster plots of the spiking activity before vs after sleep, which revealed significant improvements in sequence completion. These results are summarized in (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Sleep replay is able to reverse the damage caused to the old memory (S1) following S1* training and can enhance S1 performance at the same time as it enhances performance of S1*.
source: Thus, we predict that sleep replay is not only able to reverse the damage caused to the old memory (S1) following S1* training, but it can enhance S1 performance at the same time as it enhances performance of S1*.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: After SWS, the width of the distribution of net synaptic weights further increased indicating that sleep changes the network connectivity to develop neurons which become strongly specific for one sequence or another.
source: After SWS, the width of the distribution further increased indicating that sleep, similar to interleaved training, changes the network connectivity to develop neurons which become strongly specific for one sequence or another (Figure 5D, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The synaptic weight-based directionality index increased after sleep.
source: The synaptic weight-based directionality index that summarizes these changes (see above and Methods and Materials for details) also increased after sleep (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In experiments with a rat running on a belt in a VR apparatus, training the backward direction after training the forward one can damage (erase) the effect of forward training, however, SWS following training can reverse the damage.
source: Our study predicts that in experiments with a rat running on a belt in a VR apparatus, training the backward direction after training the forward one can damage (erase) the effect of forward training, however, SWS following training can reverse the damage.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: Directionality index should increase after SWS in experiments with a rat running on a belt in a VR apparatus.
source: Additionally, similar to interleaved training (Navratilova et al., 2012), directionality index should increase after SWS.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results and comparison to prior experimental work.

claim: Performance for S1 improved after first episode of sleep (initial consolidation).
source: Thus, performance for S1 improved after first episode of sleep (initial consolidation) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Training new memory S1* in the same population of neurons damaged S1 and led to improvement of S1*.
source: Training new memory S1* in the same population of neurons damaged S1 and led to improvement of S1*.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Training S1* took longer to achieve a high level of performance when S1 was previously consolidated during sleep, consistent with empirical results on proactive interference.
source: Consistent with empirical results on proactive interference (McDevitt et al., 2015), training S1* took longer in that scenario to achieve a high level of performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results and citation to prior work on proactive interference.

claim: Both S1 and S1* showed an improvement after a subsequent episode of sleep.
source: Finally, both S1 and S1* showed an improvement after a subsequent episode of sleep (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The training paradigm 'S1→ sleep→ S1*→ sleep' shows qualitatively similar results to the 'S1→ S1*→ sleep' paradigm.
source: Thus, the training paradigm 'S1→ sleep→ S1*→ sleep' shows qualitatively similar results to the 'S1→ S1*→ sleep' paradigm.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of modeling results from different training protocols.

claim: This result is consistent with the 'Complementary Learning Systems Theory' prediction that the old memories interfering with new learning have to be replayed during new phase of memory consolidation to avoid forgetting.
source: This result is also consistent with the 'Complementary Learning Systems Theory' prediction that the old memories interfering with new learning have to be replayed during new phase of memory consolidation to avoid forgetting (McClelland et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: After sleep, each pair of neurons preferentially supported only one sequence, S1 or S1*.
source: This analysis revealed two important properties. First, after sleep, each pair of neurons preferentially supported only one sequence, S1 or S1* (note that the connectivity matrix in Figure 6B is strictly asymmetric).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Individual neurons can be divided into two groups - those participating reliably in only one sequence replay (either S1 or S1*) and those participating in both sequences replays.
source: Second, individual neurons can be divided into two groups - those participating reliably in only one sequence replay (either S1 or S1*) and those participating in both sequences replays (see Figure 6B, where some target neurons (X-axis) receive input from source neurons (Y-axis) in only one network 'direction', left (blue) or right (red), and others receive input from both 'directions').
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Both sequences show similar high number of replays across all Up states, suggesting that both sequences are replayed during each Up state.
source: Note that both sequences show similar high number of replays across all Up states, suggesting that both sequences are replayed during each Up state.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Partial replays of both sequences occur during the same Up state, that is, any given Up state participates in replay of both memories.
source: This revealed fluctuations from one Up state to another, but the count remained high for both S1 and S1* confirming our prediction that partial replays of both sequences occur during the same Up state, that is, any given Up state participates in replay of both memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: One Up state would replay more S1 synapses, while another one (commonly next one) would replay more S1* synapses.
source: Still, zoom-in to the replay count diagram (Figure 6C, right) revealed an antiphase oscillation, that is, one Up state would replay more S1 synapses, while another one (commonly next one) would replay more S1* synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: More replay events happened during the first half of any given Up state (particularly near the Down to Up transition) compared to the second half.
source: Comparing replays during first vs second half of an Up state, we found that more replay events happened during the first half of any given Up state (particularly near the Down to Up transition) compared to the second half (not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the modeling results.

claim: Memory replay is strongest at the Down to Up state transition.
source: This result is consistent with electrophysiological data suggesting that memory replay is strongest at the Down to Up state transition (Johnson et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Many neurons participated reliably in only one sequence replay, S1 or S1*, while a few neurons participated equally in replay of both sequences, creating 'network hubs'.
source: While we found that many neurons (blue or red) participated reliably in only one sequence replay, S1 or S1*, a few neurons (green) participated equally in replay of both sequences, creating 'network hubs'.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: After S1 training, the weights for S1 strengthened (shifted to the right), while the weights for S1* weakened (shifted to the left).
source: After S1 training, the weights for S1 strengthened (shifted to the right), while the weights for S1* weakened (shifted to the left).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: After sleep, for each sequence (S1 or S1*) there was a subset of synapses that were further strengthened, while the rest of synapses were weakened.
source: After sleep, for each sequence (S1 or S1*) there was a subset of synapses that were further strengthened, while the rest of synapses were weakened (Figure 7A, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Sleep promotes competition between synapses, so that specific subsets of synapses uniquely representing each memory trace can reach the upper bound to maximize recall performance while other synapses would become extinct to minimize interference.
source: This suggests that sleep promotes competition between synapses, so that specific subsets of synapses uniquely representing each memory trace can reach the upper bound to maximize recall performance while other synapses would become extinct to minimize interference.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Sleep effectively converted recurrent connections into unidirectional connections which preferentially contributed to one memory sequence or another.
source: Sleep appears to have taken most of the weights located in the center of the plot (i.e., strongly bidirectional synapses) and separated them by pushing them to the opposite corners (K01, green box, and K10, purple box) (Figure 7B, right). In doing so, sleep effectively converted recurrent connections into unidirectional connections which preferentially contributed to one memory sequence or another.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Interleaved training resulted in similar separation of weights such that some previously recurrent synapses became functionally unidirectional.
source: It should be noted that interleaved training resulted in similar separation of weights such that some previously recurrent synapses became functionally unidirectional (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Interleaved training retained more recurrent weights than sleep likely contributing to the smaller improvement in performance during post-interleaved training testing.
source: Interleaved training, however, retained more recurrent weights than sleep likely contributing to the smaller improvement in performance during post-interleaved training testing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of modeling results for sleep vs interleaved training.

claim: The mean strength of all recurrent connections in the trained region decreased slightly during sleep.
source: The mean strength of all recurrent connections in the trained region decreased slightly during sleep (Figure 7C), however the standard deviation increased significantly (see dashed lines in Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The standard deviation of recurrent connection strength increased significantly during sleep.
source: The mean strength of all recurrent connections in the trained region decreased slightly during sleep (Figure 7C), however the standard deviation increased significantly (see dashed lines in Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Sleep effectively converts recurrent connections into unidirectional ones.
source: The last reflected strong asymmetry of the connection strength for recurrent pairs after sleep, again indicating that sleep effectively converts recurrent connections into unidirectional ones.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The mean strength of all unidirectional connections increased during sleep.
source: Indeed, the mean strength of all unidirectional connections increased during sleep (Figure 7D, blue and red lines).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: After sleep, the number of recurrent connections dropped to just about 15% of what it was after training.
source: After sleep, the number of recurrent connections dropped to just about 15% of what it was after training.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Sleep decreases the density of recurrent connections and increases the density of unidirectional connections, both by increasing the strength of anatomical unidirectional connections and by converting anatomical recurrent connections to functionally unidirectional connections.
source: Together these results suggest that sleep decreases the density of recurrent connections and increases the density of unidirectional connections, both by increasing the strength of anatomical unidirectional connections and by converting anatomical recurrent connections to functionally unidirectional connections.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Sleep allows the assignment of individual neurons to unique memories, that is, orthogonalization of memory representations, so that multiple memories could replay without interference during the same Up states of slow oscillations and can be recalled successfully after sleep.
source: This allows the assignment of individual neurons to unique memories, that is, orthogonalization of memory representations, so that multiple memories could replay without interference during the same Up states of slow oscillations and can be recalled successfully after sleep.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Sleep resulted in the orthogonalization of memory representations regardless of whether LTP/LTD ratio was biased towards LTD or LTP.
source: We found that in both cases, sleep resulted in the orthogonalization of memory representations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sleep increases the density of the memory specific connections between neurons regardless of the LTP/LTD ratio.
source: The number of synapses above these thresholds were quantified in the bar plots below showing that sleep increases the density of the memory specific connections between neurons regardless of the LTP/LTD ratio (Figure 7—figure supplement 2, bottom panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The distribution of response delays became asymmetric after S1 training, symmetric again after S1* training, and finally symmetric but wider after sleep.
source: Figure 8B shows the distribution of delays at different times. As expected, it became asymmetric after S1 training (e.g., in group B more neurons responded earlier upon stimulation of group A vs stimulation of group C), symmetric again after S1* training, and finally symmetric but wider after sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Sleep increases segregation of neurons into two groups specific to each memory based on response delay.
source: The last suggests that sleep increases segregation of neurons into two groups specific to each memory based on response delay (e.g., in group B some neurons, Bn, responded earlier upon stimulation of group A vs stimulation of group C; while other neurons, Bm, responded earlier upon stimulation of group C vs stimulation of group A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The directionality index based on delays revealed an increase after S1 training, drop after S1* training, and increase again after sleep.
source: Indeed, the directionality index based on delays (Figure 8C) revealed an increase after S1 training, drop after S1* training, and increase again after sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Neurons receiving highest total synaptic inputs in specific network direction after sleep are also those who respond with shortest delay during testing recall in that direction after sleep and also those who receive the highest number of synapses demonstrating reliable replay during sleep.
source: Note that neurons receiving highest total synaptic inputs in specific network direction after sleep are also those who respond with shortest delay during testing recall in that direction after sleep and also those who receive the highest number of synapses demonstrating reliable replay during sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: There is a strong correlation between mean response delay of a neuron during stimulation of its neighboring group, total synaptic input a neuron receives from that neighboring group, and number of connections to a neuron from that neighboring group that are replayed reliably during sleep.
source: We found a strong correlation between these three measures, that is, the neurons who responded with a shortest delay during a given sequence recall after sleep are the same neurons who received strongest synaptic input in that sequence direction after sleep and were involved in most of that sequence replays during sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Initial training allocates all available neuronal/synaptic resources to a single memory.
source: Initial training allocates all available neuronal/synaptic resources to a single memory (S1) (Figure 8E, top); some neurons contribute stronger than others (light vs dart colors in Figure 8E; based on Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results illustrated in Figure 8E.

claim: Subsequent training of a competing memory progressively erases the initial memory trace by reallocating synaptic resources to the new memory.
source: Subsequent training of a competing memory (S1*) progressively erases the initial memory trace by reallocating synaptic resources to the new memory; an initial segregation of neurons is formed (Figure 8E, middle/top).
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results illustrated in Figure 8E.

claim: Continuing training of a competing memory leads to complete and irreversible damage to the old memory – catastrophic forgetting.
source: Continuing training of a competing memory (S1*) leads to complete and irreversible damage to the old memory (S1) – catastrophic forgetting (Figure 8E, middle/bottom).
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results illustrated in Figure 8E.

claim: A sleep phase implemented before the old memory is erased allows replay of both old and new memory traces; this divides resources between competing memories leading to the formation of the orthogonal memory representations which allows the co-existence of multiple memories within overlapping populations of neurons.
source: A sleep phase implemented before the old memory is erased allows replay of both old and new memory traces; this divides resources between competing memories leading to the formation of the orthogonal memory representations which allows the co-existence of multiple memories within overlapping populations of neurons (Figure 8E, bottom).
evidence: This is a summary of the modeling results illustrated in Figure 8E.

claim: Sleep can reverse catastrophic forgetting of previously learned (old) memories after damage by new training.
source: We report here that sleep can reverse catastrophic forgetting of previously learned (old) memories after damage by new training.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on the modeling results.

claim: Sleep is able to accomplish this task through spontaneous reactivation (replay) of both old and new memory traces, leading to reorganization and fine-tuning of synaptic connectivity.
source: Sleep is able to accomplish this task through spontaneous reactivation (replay) of both old and new memory traces, leading to reorganization and fine-tuning of synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results and analysis.

claim: Sleep creates unique orthogonal representations of the competing memories that allow their co-existence without interference within overlapping ensembles of neurons.
source: As a result, sleep creates unique orthogonal representations of the competing memories that allow their co-existence without interference within overlapping ensembles of neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results and analysis.

claim: Memory representations in the brain are dynamic; after each new episode of training followed by sleep, the synaptic representations of the old memories, sharing resources with the new task, may change to achieve an optimal separation among the memory traces occupying overlapping ensembles of neurons.
source: Our study predicts that memory representations in the brain are dynamic; after each new episode of training followed by sleep, the synaptic representations of the old memories, sharing resources with the new task, may change to achieve an optimal separation among the memory traces occupying overlapping ensembles of neurons.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: Sleep, by being able to directly reactivate memory traces encoded in synaptic weight patterns, provides a powerful mechanism to prevent catastrophic forgetting and enable continual learning.
source: Our study suggests that sleep, by being able to directly reactivate memory traces encoded in synaptic weight patterns, provides a powerful mechanism to prevent catastrophic forgetting and enable continual learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results.

claim: Catastrophic interference is observed when a previously trained network is required to learn new data.
source: Catastrophic interference is observed when a previously trained network is required to learn new data, e.g., a new set of patterns. When learning new data, the network can suddenly erase the memory of the old, previously learned inputs (French, 1999; Hasselmo, 2017; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work on catastrophic interference.

claim: Catastrophic interference is thought to be related to the so-called 'plasticity-stability' problem.
source: Catastrophic interference is thought to be related to the so-called 'plasticity-stability' problem.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical understanding of catastrophic interference.

claim: The 'plasticity-stability' problem comes from the difficulty of creating a network with connections which are plastic enough to learn new data, while stable enough to prevent damage to the old memories.
source: This problem comes from the difficulty of creating a network with connections which are plastic enough to learn new data, while stable enough to prevent damage to the old memories.
evidence: This is an explanation of the plasticity-stability problem.

claim: Interleaved training is a popular method for preventing interference and forgetting.
source: Another popular method for preventing interference and forgetting is to explicitly retrain or rehearse all the previously learned inputs while training the network on the new data – interleaved training (Hasselmo, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Interleaved training can prevent catastrophic forgetting resulted from sequential training of the overlapping spike patterns.
source: In agreement with these previous studies, we show that interleaved training can prevent catastrophic forgetting resulted from sequential training of the overlapping spike patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Interleaved training does not necessarily achieve optimal separation between old and new overlapping memory traces.
source: This method, however, does not necessarily achieve optimal separation between old and new overlapping memory traces.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of interleaved training and sleep results.

claim: Interleaved training requires repetitive activation of the entire memory patterns, so if different memory patterns compete for synaptic resources each phase of interleaved training will enhance one memory trace but damage the others.
source: Indeed, interleaved training requires repetitive activation of the entire memory patterns, so if different memory patterns compete for synaptic resources (as for the opposite sequences studied here) each phase of interleaved training will enhance one memory trace but damage the others.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modeling results and understanding of interleaved training.

claim: During replay during sleep only memory specific subsets of neurons and synapses may be involved in each replay episode.
source: This is in contrast to replay during sleep when only memory specific subsets of neurons and synapses may be involved in each replay episode.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of replay during sleep shown in Figure 6.

claim: There is growing evidence for the role of sleep in consolidation of newly encoded memories.
source: Though a variety of sleep functions remain to be understood, there is growing evidence for the role of sleep in consolidation of newly encoded memories (Paller and Voss, 2004; Walker and Stickgold, 2004; Oudiette et al., 2013; Rasch and Born, 2013; Stickgold, 2013; Weigenand et al., 2016; Wei et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: NREM sleep was shown to be particularly important for reactivation of declarative (hippocampus-dependent) memories.
source: Although NREM sleep was shown to be particularly important for reactivation of declarative (hippocampus-dependent) memories (Marshall et al., 2006; Mednick et al., 2013), human studies suggest that NREM sleep may be also involved in the consolidation of the procedural (hippocampus-independent) memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Human studies suggest that NREM sleep may be also involved in the consolidation of the procedural (hippocampus-independent) memories.
source: Although NREM sleep was shown to be particularly important for reactivation of declarative (hippocampus-dependent) memories (Marshall et al., 2006; Mednick et al., 2013), human studies suggest that NREM sleep may be also involved in the consolidation of the procedural (hippocampus-independent) memories.
evidence: This is a statement about human studies on NREM sleep and procedural memory.

claim: Selective deprivation of NREM sleep, but not REM sleep, reduced memory improvement for the rotor pursuit task.
source: Selective deprivation of NREM sleep, but not REM sleep, reduced memory improvement for the rotor pursuit task (Smith and MacNeill, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Following a period of motor task learning, the duration of NREM sleep and the number of sleep spindles increased.
source: Following a period of motor task learning, the duration of NREM sleep (Fogel and Smith, 2006) and the number of sleep spindles (Morin et al., 2008) increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The amount of performance increase in the finger tapping task correlated with the amount of NREM sleep, spindle density and delta power.
source: The amount of performance increase in the finger tapping task correlated with the amount of NREM sleep (Walker et al., 2002), spindle density (Nishida and Walker, 2007) and delta power (Tamaki et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Consolidation of the procedural (skilled upper-limb) memory depended on bursts of spindle activity and slow oscillations during NREM sleep.
source: In a recent animal study (Ramanathan et al., 2015), consolidation of the procedural (skilled upper-limb) memory depended on bursts of spindle activity and slow oscillations during NREM sleep.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The model of awake training and sleep consolidation presented in this study was designed to simulate learning and consolidation of procedural memory tasks.
source: The model of awake training and sleep consolidation presented in our new study was designed to simulate learning and consolidation of procedural memory tasks.
evidence: This is a statement about the design of the model.

claim: As long as damage to the old memory is not sufficient to completely erase its synaptic footprint, sleep can enable replay of both old and newer memory traces and reverse the damage while improving performance.
source: We found that as long as damage to the old memory is not sufficient to completely erase its synaptic footprint, sleep can enable replay of both old and newer memory traces and reverse the damage while improving performance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results.

claim: Replay during REM sleep may trigger synaptic weight dynamics similar to that described for NREM sleep.
source: Replay during REM sleep (Louie and Wilson, 2001) may trigger synaptic weight dynamics similar to that we described here.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the modeling results and citation to prior work on REM replay.

claim: The occurrence of memory replay during REM is supported by place cell recordings and electroencephalography studies in humans.
source: Though REM is characterized by less synchronized spiking activity, the occurrence of memory replay during REM is supported by place cell recordings (Louie and Wilson, 2001) and electroencephalography studies in humans (Atienza and Cantero, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Similar synaptic weight dynamics and orthogonalization of memory representations were observed when periodic Up/Down state oscillations were replaced by continuous REM-like spiking activity.
source: Indeed, we observed similar synaptic weight dynamics and orthogonalization of memory representations when periodic Up/Down state oscillations were replaced by continuous REM-like spiking activity.
evidence: This claim is based on additional modeling simulations.

claim: Sharp wave-ripple like input to the cortical network would trigger replay of previously learned cortical sequences during SWS.
source: While our model lacks hippocampal input, we showed previously (Wei et al., 2016; Sanda et al., 2019) that sharp wave-ripple (SWR) like input to the cortical network would trigger replay of previously learned cortical sequences during SWS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' prior work.

claim: Replay driven by hippocampal inputs may reorganize the cortical synaptic connectivity in a matter similar to spontaneous replay.
source: This suggests, in agreement with (Skelin et al., 2019), that replay driven by hippocampal inputs may reorganize the cortical synaptic connectivity in a matter similar to spontaneous replay we described here.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the modeling results and citation to prior work.

claim: The model predicts the possibility of the partial sequence replays, that is, when short snippets of a sequence are replayed independently, within the cortex.
source: Our model predicts the possibility of the partial sequence replays, that is, when short snippets of a sequence are replayed independently, within the cortex.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: Reliable partial replays of overlapping memory traces can occur during the same cortical Up state.
source: Furthermore, we showed that reliable partial replays of overlapping memory traces can occur during the same cortical Up state.
evidence: This is based on the analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Recent data have shown evidence for partial memory replay during NREM sleep.
source: Indeed, recent data (Ghandour et al., 2019) have shown evidence for partial memory replay during NREM sleep (also see Swanson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent experimental work.

claim: The critical synaptic weight information from previous episodes of learning is still preserved after new training even if recall performance for the older task is significantly reduced.
source: Importantly, our model of sleep consolidation predicts that the critical synaptic weight information from previous episodes of learning is still preserved after new training even if recall performance for the older task is significantly reduced.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: Spontaneous activity during sleep combined with unsupervised plasticity can trigger reactivation of the previously learned memory patterns and modify synaptic weights reversing damage from the new learning.
source: Because of this, spontaneous activity during sleep combined with unsupervised plasticity can trigger reactivation of the previously learned memory patterns and modify synaptic weights reversing damage from the new learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the modeling results.

claim: The apparent loss of performance for older tasks in the artificial neuronal networks after new training – catastrophic forgetting – may not imply irreversible loss of information.
source: It further suggests that the apparent loss of performance for older tasks in the artificial neuronal networks after new training – catastrophic forgetting – may not imply irreversible loss of information as it is generally assumed.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the modeling results.

claim: Simulating a sleep-like phase in feedforward artificial networks trained using backpropagation can provide a solution for the catastrophic forgetting problem.
source: Indeed, our recent work (Krishnan et al., 2019) revealed that simulating a sleep-like phase in feedforward artificial networks trained using backpropagation can provide a solution for the catastrophic forgetting problem in agreement with our results from the biophysical model presented here.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' prior work.

claim: Relative hyperpolarization of the pyramidal neurons and increasing strength of excitatory synaptic connectivity are critical to accomplish the goal of preventing catastrophic forgetting during sleep.
source: Few changes to the network properties, normally associated with transition to sleep, were critical to accomplish this goal: relative hyperpolarization of the pyramidal neurons and increasing strength of excitatory synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results and prior work.

claim: Relative hyperpolarization of pyramidal neurons and increasing strength of excitatory synaptic connectivity are both associated with known effects of neuromodulators during wake-sleep transitions.
source: Both are associated with known effects of neuromodulators during wake-sleep transitions (McCormick, 1992) and were previously implemented in the thalamocortical model (Krishnan et al., 2016) that we used in our new study.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: These changes would make neurons relatively less excitable and, at the same time, increase contribution of the strongest synapses, effectively enhancing the dynamical range for the trained synaptic patterns and reducing contribution of synaptic noise; together this would promote replay of the previously learned memories.
source: Interestingly, these changes would make neurons relatively less excitable and, at the same time, increase contribution of the strongest synapses, effectively enhancing the dynamical range for the trained synaptic patterns and reducing contribution of synaptic noise; together this would promote replay of the previously learned memories.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism by which sleep promotes replay.

claim: The 'Sleep Homeostasis Hypothesis' suggests that homeostatic mechanisms active during sleep should result in a net synaptic depression to renormalize synaptic weights and to stabilize network dynamics.
source: The 'Sleep Homeostasis Hypothesis' (Tononi and Cirelli, 2014) suggests that homeostatic mechanisms active during sleep should result in a net synaptic depression to renormalize synaptic weights and to stabilize network dynamics.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: When synaptic plasticity during sleep was explicitly biased towards LTD, sleep was still able to selectively increase a subset of synaptic weights, thus making them memory specific, while reducing the strength of other synapses.
source: However, when synaptic plasticity during sleep was explicitly biased towards LTD, sleep was still able to selectively increase a subset of synaptic weights, thus making them memory specific, while reducing the strength of other synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: This mechanism may aid in increasing the memory capacity of the network by only strengthening the minimal number of connections required for the preservation of memories and resetting other synapses towards baseline strength during sleep.
source: We predict that this mechanism may aid in increasing the memory capacity of the network by only strengthening the minimal number of connections required for the preservation of memories and resetting other synapses towards baseline strength during sleep.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: Memory replay during SWS occurs predominantly near the Down to Up state transitions.
source: There are evidences that memory replay during SWS occurs predominantly near the Down to Up state transitions (Johnson et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Sharp-wave ripples tend to occur at the Down to Up state transition.
source: It has been shown that sharp-wave ripples tend to occur at the Down to Up state transition (Sanda et al., 2019; Skelin et al., 2019), which may explain the predomiance of the hippocampus driven replay at the beginning of cortical Up states.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cortical memory traces tend to replay more during the initial phase of an Up state, possibly because of the higher firing rate, but replay continues throughout the entire Up state duration.
source: We found that such cortical memory traces also tend to replay more during the initial phase of an Up state, possibly because of the higher firing rate, but replay continues throughout the entire Up state duration.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results.

claim: Hippocampal dependent replay of new memories, that are not yet encoded in the cortex, may occur earlier in the Up state compared to the spontaneous replay of the old memory traces, which may occur later in the Up state.
source: This predicts that hippocampal dependent replay of new memories, that are not yet encoded in the cortex, may occur earlier in the Up state compared to the spontaneous replay of the old memory traces, which may occur later in the Up state.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: Running in one direction on a linear track would lead to backwards receptive field expansion.
source: Specifically, our model predicts: (a) running in one direction on a linear track would lead to backwards receptive field expansion (confirmed for hippocampus [Mehta et al., 1997]);
evidence: This is a prediction that is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Forwards and backwards running on a linear track would lead to developing asymmetric receptive fields for different neurons.
source: (b) forwards and backwards running on a linear track would lead to developing asymmetric receptive fields for different neurons (confirmed for hippocampus [Navratilova et al., 2012]);
evidence: This is a prediction that is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Running on a belt track in a VR apparatus first only in one direction and then in reverse one could damage the learning associated with first task.
source: (c) running on a belt track in a VR apparatus first only in one direction and then in reverse one could damage the learning associated with first task;
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: SWS implemented after training would reverse damage and further enhance task specificity of neurons.
source: (d) SWS implemented after training would reverse damage and further enhance task specificity of neurons.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: Backwards expansion of the place fields was reset between sessions in CA1.
source: It is important to note that (Mehta et al., 1997) found that backwards expansion of the place fields was reset between sessions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The resetting of the backwards expanded place fields between sessions was a phenomenon specific to the CA1 and place fields did not reset in CA3.
source: Later, (Roth et al., 2012) found that the resetting of the backwards expanded place fields between sessions was a phenomenon specific to the CA1 and place fields did not reset in CA3.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Synapses in CA3 vs CA1 may have different plasticity properties.
source: These results suggest that synapses in CA3 vs CA1 may have different plasticity properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited experimental results.

claim: The neocortex may have entirely different synaptic dynamics since its goal is long term storage as opposed to temporal memory encoding.
source: Furthermore, the neocortex may have entirely different synaptic dynamics since its goal is long term storage as opposed to temporal memory encoding.
evidence: This is a speculation about differences between hippocampus and neocortex.

claim: With successive sleep periods, cortical memories become hippocampal independent.
source: With successive sleep periods, cortical memories become hippocampal independent (Lehmann and McNamara, 2011) and this may explain why resetting of the place fields was observed in CA1 (Mehta et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The cortical (such as associate cortex) representations of the sequence memories undergo a similar form of backwards expansion as it was observed in CA1.
source: Our study predicts that the cortical (such as associate cortex) representations of the sequence memories undergo a similar form of backwards expansion as it was observed in CA1.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: This form of backwards expansion persists and even increases after sleep.
source: This form of backwards expansion, however, persists and even increases after sleep.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the modeling results.

claim: Backwards memory replay and decrease in number of memory replays over time have been observed in rat hippocampus for recent memories.
source: The phenomena of backwards memory replay and decrease in number of memory replays over time have been observed in rat hippocampus for recent memories.
evidence: This is a statement about prior experimental observations.

claim: Backwards replay is predominantly observed during a post-task awake resting period within the hippocampus.
source: Within the hippocampus, backwards replay is predominantly observed during a post-task awake resting period (Foster and Wilson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Studies of hippocampal replay found decreases in replay of familiar sequences over time, which may occur because of the hippocampal SWRs inducing persistent synaptic depression within the hippocampus.
source: The studies of hippocampal replay (O'Neill et al., 2008; Giri et al., 2019) found decreases in replay of familiar sequences over time, which may occur because of the hippocampal SWRs inducing persistent synaptic depression within the hippocampus (Norimoto et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Forward replay in the model persisted during sleep.
source: We did not observe backwards replay; rather, forward replay in the model persisted during sleep.
evidence: This is based on the modeling results.

claim: There is no definitive evidence for either backwards replay or decrease in memory replays in the cortex.
source: However, we believe there is no definitive evidence for either backwards replay or decrease in memory replays in the cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of evidence.

claim: Cortical replay of recently formed memories results in a tagging of synapses involved in consolidation of those memories by increasing their synaptic efficacy.
source: The opposite, in fact, may be true. Cortical replay of recently formed memories results in a tagging of synapses involved in consolidation of those memories by increasing their synaptic efficacy (Langille, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Tagged synapses may likely be reactivated throughout sleep thereby resulting in more cortical replay during both NREM and REM sleep.
source: These tagged synapses may likely be reactivated throughout sleep thereby resulting in more cortical replay during both NREM and REM sleep (Diekelmann and Born, 2010; Langille, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.
